auxiliary_material: The conceptual framework distinguishing predictive from prognostic biomarkers (Section 2.1) provides criteria for evaluating whether metabolite associations reflect treatment-specific benefit or general disease burden. The discussion on soluble inflammatory and immune mediators (Section 5) highlights the overlap between therapeutic immune activation and systemic inflammatory noise, which is relevant for interpreting metabolite-driven immune modulation. The review's emphasis on the need for randomized treatment-by-biomarker interaction testing (Section 7.1) sets the standard for validating any metabolite-ICI correlation.
outline_action: Retrieve the primary source cited for the SCFA association (reference 182 in the text) to extract specific concentration data and statistical details. Search for empirical studies that report quantitative serum or TME metabolite levels correlated with ICI response outcomes. Investigate whether any consensus thresholds or standardized measurement protocols for these metabolites have been proposed in subsequent literature.
remaining_gap: This material does not provide the specific physiological concentration values (e.g., µM or mg/L ranges) for SCFAs or inosine in human serum or tumor microenvironment. It confirms an association exists but does not report the quantitative thresholds or statistical metrics (e.g., hazard ratios, p-values) from the primary studies it cites. It also does not specify standardized assay methods or reference ranges for these metabolites in the context of ICI therapy.
useful_material: Section 6.3 of this review discusses circulating microbial DNA and microbiome-derived metabolites, specifically naming short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and inosine as candidate blood-accessible biomarkers. The authors report that existing literature indicates higher concentrations of fecal and plasma SCFAs were associated with longer progression-free survival in patients with solid tumors treated with nivolumab or pembrolizumab. It also notes preclinical evidence that microbiome-derived inosine can enhance response to checkpoint blockade. The text explicitly lists confounding factors influencing circulating metabolite concentrations, including diet, antibiotic exposure, geography, comorbidities, and host metabolism. It states these biomarkers remain exploratory until standardized preanalytical procedures and prospective treatment-interaction testing are established.
